title: Thank you, but I'm afraid I can't

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — A dinner invitation to Ko Zaw's home
dialogs.intro: Ko Zaw invites Ani to his home. Notice how Ani turns down the part she can't accept: she never says မဟုတ်ဘူး, but gives her reason with လို့ပါ and right away offers something else instead.

grammars.title: Inviting and accepting
body: There are two ways to invite. **…ရအောင်** (*ya.-owⁿ*) means "let's" and assumes the person inviting will take part. **…မလား** (*ma.la:*) means "would you like to …?" and is more open, leaving room to say no.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: ညစာ စားရအောင်
အိမ် လာမလား
would you like to come over?
အတူတူ သွားရအောင်
ကော်ဖီ သောက်မလား

after: ⚠️ Accepting an invitation in Burmese almost always comes with **အားနာပါတယ်** ("I feel bad imposing") — which you learned in unit 12. Accepting without it sounds too casual, as if the invitation were nothing special. Say it, and your host will answer right away with အားနာစရာ မလိုပါဘူး.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Declining without saying "no"
body: Turning something down directly with မဟုတ်ဘူး or မလိုဘူး sounds harsh in Burmese. The accepted way is to **give your reason**, ending in လို့ပါ — and that already counts as a full, polite refusal. No one will press you further.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: မအားလို့ပါ
အလုပ် ရှိလို့ပါ
နေမကောင်းလို့ပါ
နောက်တစ်ခါ ရမလား
could we do it another time?
တောင်းပန်ပါတယ်

after: A safe refusal has three parts: **thanks — reason — alternative.** ကျေးဇူးပါပဲ၊ မအားလို့ပါ၊ နောက်တစ်ခါ ရမလား — "thank you, I don't have time, could we do it another time?"

⚠️ **ကျေးဇူးပါပဲ** (*chay:-zoo:-ba-bè:*) is different from ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်. The first is often used precisely when **declining** gently — a bit like "thanks, but I'm fine" in English. Pay attention to where it comes in the conversation.

grammars.title: Turning down alcohol without spoiling the mood
body: Drinking together is part of socializing in many places in Myanmar, but refusing altogether isn't strange at all — many devout Burmese don't drink either, because one of the five ရ (precepts) forbids it.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: အရက် မသောက်ပါဘူး
ဘာသာအရ မသောက်ဘူး
I don't drink for religious reasons
လက်ဖက်ရည် သောက်မယ်

after: The key isn't refusing the drink but **still joining in**. Take a glass of tea or water, raise it with everyone else, and no one will ask again.
**ငါးပါးသီလ** (*nga:-ba:-thee-la.*) is the five precepts of Buddhism — from the Pali *pañca-sīla*. Mentioning it when you decline is understood at once, and is usually met with respect.

grammars.title: …ထားတယ် — done in advance, and the result remains
body: ထား (*hta:*, "to put, place") slots in before the sentence ending to say that the action was done **beforehand** and its result still holds.
after: This form is very handy for reassuring people: မှာထားပြီးပါပြီ ("it's already ordered") says at once that it's taken care of and there's nothing more to worry about.

sections.title: Etiquette at pagodas and in people's homes

blocks.text: The rules below aren't written down anywhere, but everyone follows them. Breaking them is rarely pointed out openly — people in Myanmar are very reluctant to embarrass a guest — so you could keep doing it for months without knowing.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ဖိနပ် ချွတ်ပါ
ခြေအိတ် ချွတ်ပါ
ဓာတ်ပုံ ရိုက်လို့ ရလား
ဝင်လို့ ရလား
အားနာစရာ မလိုပါဘူး

blocks.title: ⚠️ Five things to know before entering a pagoda
items: **Shoes AND socks come off at the gate**, not at the door of the building. The whole terrace counts as sacred ground, including the stairs and the stone courtyard — which can get very hot at midday, so come in the morning or late afternoon.
**Shoulders and knees must be covered.** Many big pagodas lend out longyi, but don't count on it. This applies to men and women alike.
**Never point the soles of your feet toward a Buddha image.** If you sit on the floor, tuck your legs to the side and back — a way of sitting that in Myanmar is called sitting "like a mermaid".
**The head is the most respected part of the body, the feet the lowest.** Don't pat anyone on the head, including small children, and don't point at anything with your foot.
**Some parts of a pagoda are open to men only.** It's a local rule still in force in some places; the notice is usually in English. If in doubt, ask: ဝင်လို့ ရလား။

blocks.title: If you're invited to a Burmese home
items: Bringing fruit or snacks is always right; your host will say you shouldn't have, and will still accept happily. That's part of the ritual, not a real refusal.
Give and receive things with **your right hand while your left hand touches your right elbow** — a sign of respect that is recognized at once and much appreciated from a foreigner.
⚠️ Don't clear your plate completely on the first serving, because your host will keep refilling it. Leaving a little is the sign that you're full — a custom shared across much of Asia.
